I think many people wonder, "What use is there in reading characters and doing arithmetic, anyway?" The purpose of this practice book is not to improve one's ability to "read or calculate," but to improve the brain's executive functions, especially ① the prefrontal cortex.

The part of the brain that truly makes us human is the prefrontal cortex. Biologically speaking, in what way are humans different from animals? When we seek the answer through brain science, we arrive at this conclusion: "Humans are living beings whose prefrontal cortex has developed to an extraordinary degree."

The prefrontal cortex contains areas responsible for different functions, and these areas give rise to a wide range of important abilities.
① Communicating with others
② Creativity (Note 3)
③ Positivity / initiative
④ Shifting one's way of thinking
⑤ Performing multiple tasks simultaneously
⑥ Short-term memory

I noticed that most of the areas in the prefrontal cortex responsible for these abilities are also activated by reading characters or performing simple calculations quickly. It is known that the neurons in the prefrontal cortex are extraordinarily "flexible" (Note 4) compared with neurons in other parts of the brain, and that a single neuron can function for multiple purposes. Therefore, I thought that if we repeatedly practiced reading and calculating to train (Note 5) the prefrontal cortex, which is active during these activities, then the other abilities controlled (Note 6) by those areas would also improve.

(Note 1) Make someone human: regard or shape someone as a "human being"

(Note 2) Area: location

(Note 3) Creativity: the ability to create something new

(Note 4) Flexible: able to change to suit each situation

(Note 5) Train: make stronger

(Note 6) Control: manage, direct

To get a good night’s sleep, a smart approach is to eat just enough to satisfy the brain and silence the signal that the stomach is hungry. Put simply, it means cleverly fooling your own brain.

So what kind of food can make the brain think you are full even if you eat only a small amount? What the brain receives as a signal that it has received enough nutrition is glucose. Glucose is a basic sugar that serves as the brain’s energy source. In other words, if you eat something that is quickly absorbed and easily digested, rapidly converted into glucose, and effectively sends a signal to the brain even in a small amount, it will not burden the stomach or interfere with sleep. The brain will be moderately satisfied, allowing you to fall asleep feeling that your stomach is satisfied.

Foods that readily turn into glucose are, quite simply, sweets. Taking a few bites of a cookie or sucking on a piece of candy is also a good approach. In European hotels, for example, it is customary to place a small piece of chocolate by the bedside. However, chocolate contains caffeine, which has an awakening effect, so it may be questionable to eat it before going to bed.

（Note 1）ごまかす: to deceive, fool

（Note 2）ほどほどに: in moderation, to a moderate degree

（Note 3）ズバリ: plainly, directly

（Note 4）覚醒作用: an awakening effect

default.p.test-13-p1.vietnamese:
The phenomenon of Japanese people who do not know Japanese—“Japanese people who do not know Japanese”—often becomes a topic of discussion. A commonly cited example is the explanation of the proverb “Being kind is not for the sake of others.” The meaning of this proverb is that “if you treat others kindly with warm concern, good things will come back to you,” or, in other words, the proverb means ① “kindness is not for the sake of others (but for one’s own sake).” However, many people seem to misunderstand and incorrectly explain this saying. Where does this misunderstanding come from? According to a friend who is very knowledgeable about grammar, the key to the error lies in the word “narazu.” Because “narazu” is an archaic expression whose modern equivalent is “dewanai” (“is not”), the original meaning is “kindness is not for the sake of others.” People misunderstood it as meaning “it is of no use to others,” which led to the misunderstanding of the proverb’s meaning. As a result, many people seem to interpret it as saying, “Even if you treat others kindly, it does them no good, so it is better not to be kind.” Classical grammar is often used in proverbs. The affirmative form of “narazu” is “nari,” which corresponds to “da / de aru” (“is”). Therefore, “narazu” is not “naranai” (“does not become / is of no use”), but “dewanai” (“is not”). From a grammatical perspective, this explanation is convincing, but at the same time, I still feel that something ② remains unresolved. Although proverbs often contain paradoxical meanings (Note 1), I cannot help thinking that behind the emergence of this “new interpretation” lies the increasingly dry and cold nature of human relationships in modern society (Note 2).

(Note 1) Paradox: Something contrary to what people ordinarily think

(Note 2) Background: What lies behind or beneath something

There is a proverb from the Kamigata region: "When the mouth smiles, good fortune comes" (Laughter brings happiness). It means that good fortune will visit a family that is always smiling brightly.

People are always seeking joy and avoiding sadness. This is a common emotional tendency in every country, but laughter is a matter of "culture." Being happy does not necessarily mean that a person will laugh, nor does being sad necessarily mean that they will cry. Feelings of happiness and the expression of laughter are not directly connected. Expressions imbued with the distinctive characteristics of a country's culture produce laughter with a character unique to that country.

①Laughter does not necessarily cross national borders. There are things that the British would never laugh at but that make us laugh uncontrollably, and the reverse can also happen. Furthermore, even Japanese laughter is not uniform. There are subtle differences between regions, and the nature of laughter also varies with age. For example, when elderly people see young girls laughing loudly at something as simple as a pair of fallen chopsticks, they may look puzzled or even annoyed.

Laughter is a highly complex human expression. That is why theories about laughter are also very difficult to define consistently.

Above all, a person of character is someone whom everyone trusts. To be trusted, one must take trustworthy actions. Rather than saying grand, beautiful words, we must gradually accumulate proper and appropriate actions. Building a relationship of trust does not require hitting a “homerun.” We only need to keep steadily and diligently hitting each ball thrown to us with a bat. More specifically, this means being punctual for appointments. If we promise to complete work, we must finish it by the agreed deadline. If we say we will attend a meeting, we must attend it. If we say we will call, we must call. If we say we will introduce someone, we must make the introduction. If we say we will send a document, we must send it. If we promise to give something, we must give it. If we say we will show something, we must not forget to show it. Each of these tasks is nothing extraordinary. They are things we can easily overlook and forget unintentionally. Yet accumulating these small actions is what creates other people’s trust in you. It is just like depositing one 100-yen or 200-yen coin at a time into an account. Just as those small sums gradually become substantial assets, the everyday act of keeping promises eventually becomes a letter of trust and enhances your character.

(Note 1) Character: The high and admirable quality or value possessed by a person or thing

(Note 2) Homerun: In baseball, a very powerful hit that sends the ball a long distance

(Note 3) Baseball bat: A bat used to hit the ball in baseball

default.p.test-16-p1.vietnamese:
① I really hate reading books. To put it extremely, books are filled with things belonging to the past. Whenever I read a book, I get swept up in it and feel as though I am moving backward, which I cannot stand. In general, I move through life by doing what people commonly call seeing things with my own eyes, hearing them with my own ears, conducting experiments, and then putting everything together to decide, “This is how it should be done.” If I encounter something I do not understand and have to read a book about it, I would rather spend that free time asking someone else. Even if I read a 500-page book, only about one page would actually be necessary. I would never do something as inefficient as rummaging through the book to find that page. My company is full of university graduates, and it is much faster to give them the problem and ask an expert in that field. Then I simply combine what I learn with my experience so far and put it into practice, thinking, “This should work.” Yet people imagine that Soichiro Honda personally did everything from A to Z. That is completely absurd.

In the end, I think my strength is simply that I can openly and straightforwardly ask other people questions. In other words, because I have clearly displayed the fact that I did not receive a proper formal education, it is not strange for me not to know something. That is why I do not need to worry about what others think and can comfortably ask anyone anything. By contrast, if I had received even a little schooling, I would be unable to set aside my pride and ask others for help because I would be afraid they would laugh and say, “You do not even know something like that?” As a result, I would ②force myself. Things I could understand immediately by asking someone else would remain beyond my grasp. Nothing could be more wasteful or uneconomical.

(Note 1) Extremely: highly distorted or one-sided

(Note 2) From A to Z: everything, from the smallest tasks to the largest

(Note 3) Open and straightforward: without hesitation or unnecessary formality

(Note 4) Unconcerned: not worrying about or paying attention to something

(Note 5) Halfhearted, a little: even something small can become incomplete or awkward when done halfway

default.p.test-18-p1.vietnamese:
How should you praise a subordinate? People often say that praise helps nurture and develop people, but depending on how it is given, it may have the opposite effect.

Columbia University psychologist Claudia Mueller divided elementary school students aged 10 to 12 into two groups and studied the effects of different forms of praise.

First, after the children took several kinds of tests, she praised the first group by saying, "You did very well because you are talented." She praised the second group by saying, "You did very well because you worked hard."

She then gave them another test and announced to everyone this time, "Your results were poor." After this, the children in the first group thought, "I am not talented enough," and had no desire to try again. The children in the second group, on the other hand, became highly motivated, thinking, "It is because I did not work hard enough. I will try harder next time."

Because the children in the second group had been guided to judge that "the cause of success or failure lies in effort," when they encountered failure, they thought positively, "If I work harder, I will succeed."

This study focused on children, but it also presents a way of thinking that can be applied when praising subordinates.

（Note 1）再挑戦する (try again): to attempt something one more time

（Note 2）誘導する (guide/direct): to lead someone toward a goal

default.p.test-19-p1.vietnamese:
In Europe, there is a proverb that says, "The busier a person is, the more free time they have." This is because busy people concentrate and finish their work quickly, after which they have free time. In contrast, people with too much time on their hands handle even small tasks slowly and sluggishly. Because they never finish their work, they ultimately have no free time and feel extremely busy. This proverb expresses such a paradox.

A story like the following appears in the famous book "Parkinson's Law." An idle and wealthy old woman suddenly decided to write a postcard to her granddaughter. The granddaughter was staying at a resort to escape the heat. It took twenty minutes to find the address. It took forty-five minutes to think about what to write. Before going out to mail the completed letter, she spent another twenty minutes deciding whether to take a Western-style umbrella. Altogether, it took nearly an hour and a half. This was because she had too much time; if she had been busy, everything would have been finished in just three minutes.

Time is necessary, but having too much of it is not good at all. At the very least, one should not think that one has plenty of time.

It is better for time to be slightly scarce. We should race against time in our work and studies. Outstanding results emerge from work carried out under pressure and with intense concentration. We must always feel that we lack time—in other words, we must remain in a "time-hungry" state.

To achieve this, it is important not to set aside too much time. Even when it comes to study time, the idea that more is always better is absolutely forbidden. Instead, deliberately shorten the amount of time. Only then can you study more substantially and efficiently.

(Note 1) それにひきかえ: In contrast to that.

(Note 2) Paradox (逆説): A way of thinking that runs counter to what people normally expect.

(Note 3) 有閑 (na-adjective): Idle, with plenty of free time.

(Note 4) 富裕な: Wealthy.

(Note 5) メイ: Granddaughter.

(Note 6) しめて: In total.

(Note 7) Forbidden (禁物): Something that must not be done.

(Note 8) 充実した: Substantial, fulfilling.

This is a story from when Mr. Honda was young and went on a business trip abroad to country E. After arriving, he first contacted an employee of a business partner and arranged to meet two days later because they needed to discuss a business transaction. Two days later, he went to the agreed location, but the other person did not show up. When he tried calling, the person said, “I changed my mind. I would like to postpone the meeting until another day.” Mr. Honda was extremely surprised. He also felt very angry. He had traveled all the way there, yet the other person had unilaterally canceled the appointment with nothing more than “I changed my mind.” It was extremely rude. Furthermore, there had been no prior contact at all...

Several days later, Mr. Honda told this story to a Japanese person living locally. That person then said the following: “Things like that happen frequently in this country. Someone invited to a party may reply that they will attend. However, on the actual day of the party, they do not show up. And they do not contact anyone either. ...When people are invited, they temporarily accept even if they do not intend to attend. That is because refusing immediately at that moment is considered rude.”

After hearing this, Mr. Honda had to admit that the concept of “rudeness” takes many different forms depending on the place.

default.p.test-20-p1.vietnamese:
A
As the proverb「Time is money」says, time is extremely valuable. Express-train fares, rush laundry fees (Note 1), and express-mail charges are costs paid to save time. Saving time (Note 2) is recognized as valuable, given a price, and paid for by users.

There is also something called「early-bird fares」offered by airlines. If you buy a plane ticket early, the price is discounted. This is because the airline recognizes the value of selling the ticket early and therefore lowers its price. Indeed,「Time is money」.

Humanity has gradually learned to manage many different things, but we still cannot control time freely. That is why people must recognize the value of time and be willing to pay for it, mustn’t they?

B
There is a term called「unpaid overtime」. Since overtime means extending working hours in order to work, employees should naturally be paid for that time and labor. Although「Time is money」, receiving not even 1 yen for it is what「unpaid overtime」means. In other words, employees are「providing free labor」for the company. Although the company recognizes the value of its employees’ labor and the time they spend on it, it does not pay them for that value. Moreover, society calls it「unpaid overtime」and accepts it. It seems that the idea that「Time is money」has still not become widely accepted.

（Note 1）Rush service: Completing something in a short time

（Note 2）Shortening: Making something shorter

default.p.test-21-p1.vietnamese:
<Person seeking advice>
I am a ninth-grade girl who was accepted into my preferred high school a few days ago. I have been studying hard for entrance exams all this time, so now I want to enjoy the high school life that is about to begin as fully as possible. That is why I am planning to buy a really cute swimsuit and go to the beach this summer. However, there is one problem. I am only 148 cm tall, but I weigh as much as 55 kg. I want to lose 7 kg over the next 5 months. How can I lose weight effectively? I am determined to lose weight, so I will do my very best.

<Respondent A>
If you want to lose as much as 7 kg in five months, I think you should certainly pay attention to your diet. Your meals should center on vegetables and maintain a low calorie intake. Even if vegetables are the main component, it is important to add seaweed and processed foods such as tofu and natto to ensure a balanced intake of the nutrients your body needs, including vitamins, minerals, and protein. In addition, limit high-calorie sweets and greasy snacks. In particular, you must never eat late at night. Moderate exercise will also be necessary. If you pay attention to your diet and exercise your body, your weight will definitely go down. Keep working hard while picturing yourself wearing a cute swimsuit this summer.

<Respondent B>
Until now, you have spent all your time sitting at your desk studying, so perhaps you have not had much time to exercise. When you enter high school, I strongly recommend joining a sports club. That is a way to exercise and burn calories. As for food, do not eat an unbalanced diet; eat a variety of foods. You are only 15 and still growing, so of course you need vegetables, but you also need to eat enough meat and fish. Instead of cutting calories, you should burn off excess calories. For that purpose, exercise. One more thing: I think maintaining a regular, disciplined lifestyle is very important. Go to bed early, get up early, pay attention to your mealtimes, and eat three full meals at fixed times. Do not eat anything after 9 p.m. The basic principle is that if you lead a healthy life, you will have a well-balanced, healthy figure (Note 1). Even if you do not lose 7 kg in five months, I think you can still become attractive.

(Note 1) Figure, proportions: The balance of the body, such as height and leg length.

＜Question / Discussion topic＞
As the economy worsens, and people think about their children’s future higher education and employment, voices are increasingly being heard everywhere saying that having and raising children is very difficult. More and more people are struggling with the question of whether to have children. At the same time, the national and local governments have begun implementing measures to provide financial support to families with young children, make it easier to take leave from work, and create better conditions for raising children. What do you think about raising children?

＜Respondent A＞
When I got married, I thought I did not want to have to quit my job because of raising children. Recently, however, it has become easier at my workplace to take leave to care for children, the number of part-time jobs has increased, and understanding toward people raising young children has continued to improve. My husband has also become more cooperative and provides more support with housework and childcare. Thanks to government policies, I feel that society is changing in a positive direction.

＜Respondent B＞
When I was young, my parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and neighbors all helped raise children together. Nowadays, however, fewer people live with their grandparents, and interaction with neighbors has also decreased. My spouse and I are in the same situation: leaving our child home alone all day while we work feels dangerous, but asking someone else to look after the child costs money and is economically difficult.

＜Respondent C＞
Recently, supermarkets, libraries, and bookstores have added play areas for children, and public facilities now have dedicated spaces for breastfeeding babies, which is very welcome and appreciated. However, there are still not enough preschools, and there is also the problem of bullying in schools, so many things remain a source of anxiety. Education costs are also a major burden, so I do not think we can say that the environment for raising children has become better.

default.p.test-23-p1.vietnamese:
＜A’s opinion＞
It is a mistake to think that reading manga will lead children to do nothing but play. Don’t people also learn things from reading manga? Recently, people have said that children no longer read books, but manga provide an opportunity to read written language. Even when they encounter unfamiliar kanji, they can usually learn how to read them because kana are provided. Expressions such as idioms and proverbs also become easier to understand in manga, so manga might even be useful in Japanese-language classes. I think some people argue that ①if students bring manga to school, they might secretly read them during class. However, isn’t that something that depends on the guidance and instruction of teachers and parents? I think this would also be a good opportunity to teach children to clearly distinguish when they may read manga and when they may not.

＜B’s opinion＞
Some people say,「If reading manga increases opportunities to read written language, it will help students learn kanji and vocabulary. Therefore, bringing manga to school is not a bad thing」, but is that really true?

I do think that idioms and proverbs become easier to understand in manga, but the claim that kanji with furigana helps students learn how to read them is not so convincing in practice. From my own experience, when kana are provided, people feel reassured and simply skim past the kanji, which means that, on the contrary, they no longer bother to remember how to read them.

Furthermore, people say that if children are taught to distinguish the boundary, they will not read manga during class, but I am extremely skeptical about whether such guidance and instruction can actually be carried out.

（Note 1）けじめをつける: to clearly and decisively distinguish between what is right and what is wrong.

default.p.test-24-p1.vietnamese:
Before entering university, I worked at a small manufacturing plant for three years.

There, I met many people, learned how to do the work from them, and learned a great deal about the ways of the world.

Having lived in the real world made the subjects I later studied for the university entrance examination extremely easy to understand.

Since the university I applied to was private, there were only three examination subjects: Japanese, social studies, and a foreign language. I was able to manage the social studies and Japanese examinations largely because of the books I had read while working.

In this way, remembering things by anchoring them in concrete experiences from the real world allows knowledge to sink much more deeply into us.

Parents and teachers often tend to think that moving straight on to a higher level of education is the most effective path. However, people who take a detour—for example, those whose progress is delayed by a year because of illness—often develop greater maturity as human beings.

The son of someone I know traveled alone, during his final year of high school, from inland China through Pakistan and Turkey, toured European countries such as France, and hitchhiked across the continent all the way to Portugal's Atlantic coast.

The experience of meeting many people in those places seems to have become an advantage in his later studies. Some middle and high school students also travel through many countries on the Peace Boat, meeting all kinds of people.

Such real-life experiences are far more meaningful than sitting at a desk and memorizing historical timelines. Without even going abroad, people can cycle all around Japan. The current way of thinking that education consists only of studying at a desk is becoming an obstacle to cultivating richer human character.

Today, people often say that human life lasts eighty years. Of those years, middle school accounts for only three short years. Therefore, it is absolutely not the case that everything in a person's life is determined during those three years of middle school.

Recently, children have stopped helping with housework.

This is because more and more parents think it is better for their children to study than to do such chores. However, many adults today helped their families with housework when they were young.

That certainly did not become useless in their lives.

(Note 1) Kiwamete: extremely, very

(Note 2) Sutoreeto ni: directly, straightforwardly, in one continuous movement

(Note 3) Hitchhike: traveling by asking passing vehicles for a ride

(Note 4) Peace Boat: an activity involving travel by ship to many countries and interaction with people

(Note 5) Historical timeline: a table arranging historical events in chronological order

It was quite some time ago. When a committee on road traffic was established within the National Police Agency, I attended its first meeting. At the time, the secretariat explained as follows.

「In recent years, the roads in Tokyo and other major cities have become extremely congested. Therefore, we have established this committee to address the problem of traffic congestion.」

So I asked:

「I see. Then what results would this committee have to produce in order to be considered successful?」

Unless the criteria for evaluation—or what could be called the rules—were clearly defined, I would not know how to carry out the work. I wanted to clarify what results would constitute success—in other words, what exactly needed to be optimized.

When I repeatedly pressed them for an answer, the other side became angry. Finally, they blurted out: 「As long as the traffic congestion on Tokyo’s roads is gone, that’s good enough, isn’t it?」

So I immediately replied:

「Reduce traffic congestion on Tokyo’s roads? That’s easy. Turn all the traffic lights for roads leading out of Tokyo green, and turn all the traffic lights for roads leading into Tokyo red. Then, once people leave, they will not be able to come back in. Tokyo will become completely empty, and the congestion will disappear instantly.」

Some people might get annoyed and say that I was being flippant and unserious, but I was not speaking carelessly out of sheer desperation. My point was that there are many different ways to reduce congestion, even when we use the same expression.

For example, at a certain intersection, only 800 cars have been able to pass through in one hour. If a new approach makes it possible for 1,000 cars to pass, that could be considered a reduction in congestion. Traffic-control measures could be designed to create such a flow of vehicles.

On the other hand, there is another possible approach. Until now, it may have taken at least 30 minutes to travel from an intersection to a certain destination. If a new approach makes it possible to reach the destination in 15 minutes, that too could be regarded as a reduction in congestion. This would be an approach aimed at shortening travel time as much as possible. Traffic-control methods will change depending on which measure or evaluation standard is used. That is why it is essential to decide on the evaluation scale first.

This is extremely important. If we discuss matters vaguely without clarifying the specific objective, the result will often fail to meet expectations. Japanese people are very skilled at using language, but for that very reason, they often act without precisely defining the meanings of the words they use.

(Note 1) 発足する: to begin operating, to be established and launched

(Note 2) 混雑を緩和する: to alleviate congestion

(Note 3) やけくそになって: becoming reckless or giving up and thinking that anything goes

(Note 4) 指摘する: to point out something problematic

(Note 5) 尺度: measure, evaluation standard

(Note 6) クリアにする: to clarify, to make clear

(Note 7) 思わしくない: not very good, not as expected

(Note 8) 定義する: to define the meaning of a word clearly

default.p.test-26-p1.vietnamese:
The meeting was originally intended to bring everyone together to generate ideas freely, but when it actually took place, it ended up with results such as “few people speaking,” “no lively discussion,” or “nothing more than the exchange of information and reports.” Surely we have all experienced this kind of situation before.

Why does this happen? Is it really that no one can speak up? What is needed for everyone to voluntarily offer comments and opinions? ①At times like these, this is the line often used by the facilitator or a superior: “Anything is fine, so go ahead and share an idea.” Does this kind of urging actually work? Unfortunately, it rarely seems to be effective. Companies with an environment where people are truly free to say anything are extremely rare, and in a company like that, this line would never be uttered in the first place. “You say anything is fine, but what am I supposed to say? Would it be okay if I said you should quit...?” At most, participants can only grumble such useless complaints to themselves. Unless they understand the “purpose” of the situation, they will not know what to say. Therefore, “clarifying the purpose” is also an essential prerequisite here. Furthermore, we must carefully consider the reasons why few people speak up. There may be many different cases, but don’t you also feel that thoughts such as “I haven’t organized my ideas yet, so I can’t speak,” “What if people think I’m stupid if I say this?” and “If I let this slip, the work will be pushed back onto the person who proposed it” are preventing people from speaking? In other words, some kind of self-protective awareness is causing them to remain silent. ②Surely all of us have had this experience. If anyone claims never to have thought this way, perhaps they should question whether they themselves are creating a “one-person show.”

When people are highly defensive, pressuring them even more to “share an opinion” only makes them reinforce their defenses.

Anxiety and fear hinder many of people’s actions and statements. As a result, frank actions and statements become even more difficult. What is needed is to create a safe environment. It is extremely important to build a space where whatever someone says will be accepted. Naturally, there will also be opposing or critical opinions in a discussion. However, the opinion must first be received as a valuable contribution. Any objections or suggestions can come afterward. Whether an organization has the habit of “always accepting an idea once” will determine whether its discussions become lively.

(Note 1) Line: Words or a statement.

(Note 2) Soil: Environment.

(Note 3) Extremely rare: Very uncommon, almost nonexistent.

(Note 4) To grumble: To utter useless complaints that solve nothing even when expressed.

(Note 5) Maximum limit: The extent to which something can be done.

(Note 6) Initiator: The first person to say or propose something.

(Note 7) Defense: Preventing danger and protecting oneself.

(Note 8) Defensive posture: Preventing danger and protecting oneself.

(Note 9) Hinder: To obstruct, disturb, or annoy.

default.p.test-27-p1.vietnamese:
① Buying a ¥1,000 item for ¥500
② Buying a ¥1,010,000 item for ¥1,000,000
Which of the two examples above represents the better deal?

Buying a ¥1,000 item for ¥500 makes us feel as though we have gained twice as much. Indeed, in percentage terms, the price has been reduced by as much as 50%.

By contrast, when buying a ¥1,010,000 item for ¥1,000,000, the discount is less than 1%, and in terms of the amount of money, ¥1,010,000 and ¥1,000,000 do not feel all that different.

But stop and think carefully: you are actually saving ¥10,000! Faced with that amount, whether you gain or lose ¥500 no longer seems important.

For this reason, I decided to overlook gains and losses on purchases of less than ¥10,000 and focus only on large purchases.

In other words, cost reduction should not be considered in percentages but in absolute amounts.

People who lack this kind of policy regarding money often think, when buying an expensive item, “¥1,010,000 and ¥1,000,000 are practically the same, so I’ll just go with the one the store employee recommended.”

This psychological background may be why expenses tend to soar when people buy a house or hold a wedding. The store may say, “Buying a house is a once-in-a-lifetime event,” or “You only have one wedding in your life,” and somehow we end up thinking, “It’s okay if it costs a little more.” Ironically, these same people may haggle over every ¥10 when shopping at a supermarket. That is rather amusing/interesting (①).

Put this way, I may be criticized with words such as, “Saving every ¥10 is important. Haven’t people always said, ‘Many small things add up to something great’ (Note 7)?”

However, even if you save ¥10 every day, you will save only ¥3,650 in a year. Saving ¥10,000 just once a year would therefore be far more effective. Some people say, “It’s fine to be frugal normally, but you should splurge once in a while,” but this is a rather dangerous way of thinking (②).

For example, if you save ¥100 every day and occasionally splurge ¥50,000 at once, the result is:
100 (yen) × 365 (days) － 50,000 (yen) ＝ △13,500 yen
(△ indicates a negative amount.)

Unfortunately, the result is a deficit—a loss. People like this are naturally prone to running deficits and are therefore unsuitable for running a business. In short, they merely feel as though they have saved money without accurately recognizing their household’s financial situation.

(Note 1) 得する: to benefit financially—after doing something, to have more money left than before.

(Note 2) 削減: reduction, cutting back

(Note 3) ポリシー: policy, basic principle guiding one’s actions

(Note 4) 購入: purchase, buying something

(Note 5) 背景: background, what lies behind something

(Note 6) ケチる: to be stingy, to be unwilling to spend money

(Note 7) チリも積もれば山となる: Many small things add up to something great.

default.p.test-28-p1.vietnamese:
When one actually sets about compiling and summarizing material, one realizes that it is quite a laborious and difficult task. People who have struggled with that troublesome process gradually tend to avoid organizing their thoughts or putting them into writing. Instead, they bury themselves in reading. The more they read, the more their knowledge increases. Their reference material continues to accumulate, but for precisely that reason, compiling it becomes even more complicated and difficult. In this way, people are produced who are highly educated and extremely diligent in their studies, yet leave behind almost no complete work or finished publication.

"I need to polish and ponder my ideas a little more before I can start writing..." This is what students preparing to write their graduation theses often say. If they keep hesitating, time gradually runs out, and impatience and panic begin to set in. How could any good ideas emerge from a mind in a state of frantic panic?

At such times, I usually advise them, "In any case, just try writing something." Perhaps, deep down, they are afraid to begin writing. So they make up reasons and excuses for themselves, putting off taking up their pens day after day. Meanwhile, their impatience and panic as the deadline approaches continue to grow.

No matter how much they think aimlessly about all sorts of things, neither coherence nor direction emerges. Everything remains confused and vague. In particular, when they research too thoroughly and accumulate an excessive amount of reference material, the confusion becomes even more pronounced. "I cannot possibly start writing while things are still like this; I need to prepare a more solid outline first"—this is the common mindset of many people preparing to write a thesis. That is a bad approach.

Just relax and start by trying to write. The essential point is not to tense up or put excessive pressure on yourself to produce a great thesis. The more you strain and force yourself, the less likely it is to become a masterpiece; instead, it may end up as a superficial, long-winded epic with no substance. Surely everyone wants to write a good work, but simply wanting to write one does not mean that one will be able to produce it. On the contrary, once you abandon the excessive desire to write something great, everything proceeds more smoothly. The same applies not only to theses but also to reports and essays.

(Note 1) てこずる: To struggle with something because it is exceptionally difficult

(Note 2) 敬遠する: To avoid something, be reluctant to do it

(Note 3) 焦燥: Impatience, restlessness, agitation

(Note 4) 混沌とした: Confused, vague, lacking clarity

(Note 5) いちじるしい: Clearly visible, markedly evident

(Note 6) 気負う: To strain oneself, be determined to do something exceptionally well

(Note 7) 力作: An outstanding work, a painstakingly produced masterpiece

(Note 8) 上すべりした: Superficial, shallow

default.p.test-29-p1.vietnamese:
Although this practice has become somewhat less common recently, the beginning of a letter is traditionally expected to contain a seasonal greeting.

“Now that the maple leaves have begun to change color, I trust that you are continuing to live in good health. Thanks to the blessings of heaven, everyone here is also doing well.”

These are the kinds of words used as a greeting. Omitting this section is considered a form of abbreviation, in which case the letter begins with words such as “Prefatory remarks omitted.” A woman might write something like, “Please forgive me for omitting the prefatory remarks.”

The idea that beginning a letter immediately with its main subject is impolite and crude probably reflects ①a certain aspect of the Japanese mentality. The opening remarks naturally have no substantial meaning. They are simply nice to have. Without them, people feel that something is missing.

Europeans and Americans do not add such opening remarks to their letters. They say that when Japanese people write things such as “Please forgive me for the impudence of sending this letter so suddenly,” it is strange to apologize in advance, because from the recipient’s perspective, a letter from someone writing for the first time is always “sudden.”

②The same applies even in face-to-face conversation. Suppose we cannot accept what the other person is saying. Even when we have no choice but to express our disagreement clearly, if we begin by saying, “I cannot agree with what you are saying,” there is a risk that we will be perceived as extremely confrontational. It would be unbearable to be seen that way. That is why we have to place a “cushion” between ourselves and the other person. That is what an opening remark does.

“Your opinion is very interesting. I had never thought about it that way before, but hearing you say it, I feel that you may indeed be right...”

After first surrounding the conversation with words that sound completely agreeable and supportive, we then calmly and gradually begin to reveal our opposing view:

“But could there perhaps be a case like this...?”

We must not rush straight to the conclusion. Recently, the expression “To state the conclusion...” has become popular among some people, but it may be difficult for such an approach to reach the hearts of sensitive listeners.

The truth is difficult to say. People naturally feel that way. Therefore, they give a preface, take a breath, and then begin addressing the main topic, but even so, they do not suddenly jump straight to the conclusion. They carefully approach it little by little from the outside. Ideally, it would be best not to have to say the difficult thing at all. Better still, the other person might sense and understand it without our having to say it. A person who can show such empathy and sensitivity is truly someone who understands how to conduct themselves.

(Note 1) のっけ: the very beginning
(Note 2) はしたない: ill-mannered, impolite
(Note 3) まくらのことば: words spoken before entering the main subject; an opening remark
(Note 4) 承服できない: unable to accept or agree with something
(Note 5) 挑戦的: having a strong attitude that seems ready to confront the other person
(Note 6) クッション: something placed between people to soften the harshness of an interaction; a cushion
(Note 7) おもむろに: calmly, unhurriedly
(Note 8) 察する: to infer and understand the other person’s feelings

default.p.test-3-p1.vietnamese:
While waiting for a train, I looked at a vending machine selling drinks. The vending machine stocked things such as fruit juice, tea, and drinks in aluminum cans or plastic bottles, but all of the containers were cylindrical. Why is that?

When containers with the same capacity but different shapes are compared, a sphere has the smallest surface area, and a cylinder has the second-smallest. The smaller the surface area, the less aluminum or plastic is needed. In this respect, a sphere would certainly be the most suitable shape for a container holding liquid. However, a sphere is not easy to handle when arranging or transporting it. That is probably why cylinders, which have the second-smallest surface area after spheres, are used.

(Note 1) 運搬する: To transport or carry

When people hear the word「science」, many tend to think that it is「difficult」or「hard to understand」. So why is scientific research so demanding? It is because one must understand at the same time things that initially seem unrelated to the subject being investigated but are actually closely connected to it.

When we understand one thing, we discover a「new problem」related to it. The more we investigate, the more things there are to investigate. It is like moving through a long, endless tunnel. default.p.test-7-p1.vietnamese: If we say that on clear days the temperature remains high even after night falls, that is actually not the case—the temperature drops instead. On the other hand, on cloudy days, although the sun does not appear during the day, the night becomes warm. This may sound a little strange, but it is thanks to the activity of clouds. By absorbing solar energy arriving from outside and regulating the amount of solar energy reaching the Earth's surface, while also storing the energy radiated from the ground and distributing it evenly across the entire Earth, clouds perform this temperature-regulating function. As a result, differences in the Earth's temperature and humidity are reduced, making them more uniform and stable. For this reason, we cannot necessarily say that 「when there is sunlight, it gets warmer, and when there is no sunlight, it gets colder」.

default.q.test-23-q2-2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) Aは「マンガだと、漢字の意味が勉強できるし、慣用句やことわざも勉強しやすい」と考え、Bは「マンガだと慣用句やことわざはわかりやすいが、漢字の勉強にはならない」と考えている。
Author A believes that manga is useful for studying both kanji and idioms, whereas B acknowledges that idioms and proverbs are easier to understand but argues that manga does not help with kanji study because the kana let readers feel secure and skim the text.
default.q.test-23-q2-2.explanation: The key to this question comparing viewpoints is the N2 grammar pattern 「～かというと、そうはいかない」. It often follows a conditional clause 「～ば」 and denies an expected result, meaning “if you say or think that..., the reality is not that simple or straightforward.” The decisive evidence appears in Part B, where the author argues: 「漢字にふりがながついていれば、読み方の勉強になるかというと、そうはいかない。私自身の体験から言うのだが、カナがあると安心してしまって、漢字を読み流すことになり、かえって読み方を覚えようとしなくなる。」. The complete translation is: “If you say that having furigana attached to kanji means you will learn how to read them, that is not necessarily true. Based on my own experience, when kana are provided, I feel reassured and end up skimming over the kanji, so I become even less inclined to memorize their readings.” Thus, Author A agrees that manga can help learners develop both kanji readings and idiomatic expressions (「漢字の読み方を知ることができます。慣用句やことわざなどの意味も…わかりやすくなります」), whereas Author B concedes only the benefit of learning idiomatic expressions and firmly rejects the idea that manga helps with kanji readings. A classic strategy for A-B comparison questions is not to choose based on a temporarily concessive statement such as 「たしかに～とは思うが」, but to focus on the counterargument after 「が」. Also watch for choices that reverse the condition involving “with kana” and “without kana,” such as option (c).
default.q.test-23-q2-2.why.0: ✗ (a) This is incorrect because only A claims that reading manga with kana helps learners learn kanji readings, whereas B points out that the kana merely encourages skimming and prevents readers from remembering the kanji.
default.q.test-23-q2-2.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because this option overlooks the key disagreement between A and B regarding the effectiveness of learning kanji and does not fully address the question’s connection to learning.
default.q.test-23-q2-2.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because the passage clearly states that B believes the presence of kana makes readers feel comfortable skimming and become less motivated to remember kanji, which is the complete opposite of the statement in the choice.
default.q.test-23-q2-2.why.3: ✓ (d) This correctly presents both sides' positions: A believes manga helps with both kanji and idiomatic expressions, while B acknowledges only its usefulness for idiomatic expressions and denies its effectiveness for learning kanji.
default.q.test-33-q1-1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 引き取りサービスを申し込む。送料は通信販売会社が払う。
According to the passage, customers who want to return an item must apply for a pickup service, and the mail cost for the return is paid entirely by the mail-order company.
default.q.test-33-q1-1.explanation: The title uses the formal instruction 「ご返品の場合は、引き取りサービスをご利用ください」 (In the case of a return, please use the pickup service), formed with noun + の場合は + ご + action noun + ください. This is a standard honorific expression in business communication, specifying the default procedure customers should follow. The text also clearly identifies who pays the shipping cost: 「引き取りサービスをご利用の場合、返品送料は当社が負担します」 (If you use the pickup service, our company will cover the return shipping fee). The verb 「負担する」 means to bear or pay for a cost, confirming that the customer does not have to pay it. Examinees may be distracted by the information that A is usually not at home and mistakenly choose self-shipping (choice (d)). However, the passage permits direct shipping only as an alternative when arranging a pickup is inconvenient (引き取りがご都合の悪い場合); it is not the initial procedure. For N2 information-searching reading questions, follow the highest-priority instruction at the beginning of the text before considering conditional alternatives below.
default.q.test-33-q1-1.why.0: ✗ (a) The statement that the customer pays the return fee is incorrect because the passage clearly states that when the pickup service is used, the company pays the return shipping fee (当社が負担します).
default.q.test-33-q1-1.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct, because the passage instructs customers to prioritize using the pickup service (引き取りサービス), and the seller will fully bear the cost of return shipping.
default.q.test-33-q1-1.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because pickup service is the first-priority option, and the buyer also does not have to pay the fee when the product is defective (不良品).
default.q.test-33-q1-1.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect because direct self-shipping is only an alternative when arranging pickup is genuinely inconvenient (引き取りがご都合の悪い場合). The designated default method remains door-to-door pickup service.
